author: Jack Wiedner
title: Revived Brooklyn Center Little League starts taking shape - NewsBreak
text:
By Jack Wiedner ,
2 days ago
The grassroots effort to revive Brooklyn Center Little League just took a major step forward. After a summer of fundraising and fixing up Thurs Field, the organization has regained its status as a federally recognized nonprofit — and the property is now tax-exempt.
Although BCLL still has a sizable debt to pay off, earning that tax-exempt status ensures that the organization will not rack up additional charges from the city or the county.
“If you were carrying around a backpack full of bricks, it's like you took out two bricks,” Jennifer Brenny said. “It’s a little bit lighter, but it's still there.”
Brenny described herself and the de facto leader of BCLL. She served as the team’s safety officer until their last game in 2023 and is now the driving force behind the effort to bring it back.
This summer, Brenny successfully lobbied for a five-year repayment plan that allows BCLL to spread out the financial impact of their delinquent taxes. She has spent the past few months finding creative ways to raise funds, including renting out the property to a car show in August and selling concessions at a kickball party for area youth.
Brenny hopes that the next fundraiser will yield some larger donations — because this time, they have a match. “We have been given an anonymous donation of up to $500,” she said. “If up to $2,000 is donated, they will match it at 25%.”
Unlike their property taxes, BCLL will continue to rack up monthly water and electricity bills. Brenny said $2,500 would be enough to bring them up-to-date on those payments.
In the coming months, Brenny said her priority is finding additional volunteers. Her husband, Jason, plans to help out with coaching and concessions once they establish a team. Kevin Pitman, head coach of Brooklyn Center High School baseball, is providing groundskeeping services and plans to step up as the team’s maintenance manager.
“We’re hoping an accountant would help us as kind of a pro-bono thing, or maybe even join the board. We need to keep these taxes, our bank account and everything in order,” Brenny said.
With a repayment plan in place and a board beginning to take shape, the future of BCLL is coming into focus. For Brenny, the most important part is figuring out how to best serve the youth of Brooklyn Center.
"In order to get the kiddos involved, we need to know their interests,” she said. “We've tossed around things like Banana Ball for kids, renting out the fields for other teams or hosting tournaments.”
Popularized by an exhibition baseball team in Savannah, Georgia, Banana Ball implements unique rules and on-field antics to create faster-paced games. Following that blueprint is just one of many ways Brenny thinks BCLL could drive interest in the revived team. “There's a lot of ideas, but we need the people of the community to come together and be a part of our board to see them through,” she said.
Will it still be Little League?
BCLL is no longer recognized by Little League International, though the organization does have the opportunity to reply. Brenny said they would only do so if there is enough community interest.
Moving away from the official Little League entity would mean giving up certain perks, including the ability to play in national tournaments. However, Brenny and Pitman have both said the change could better suit the needs of the organization, allowing them to pay staff members and pursue a wider range of grants. The nearby Brooklyn Park Youth Athletic Association serves as an example of this model.
Building back up
Brooklyn Center Little League was founded nearly 60 years ago. The organization’s field was named after longtime volunteer and former president Lester Thurs, who once owned the property where the baseball diamond now stands. When he passed away in 2002, the property at 6030 Vincent Ave. N. was placed into a trust under the condition that it must always be used for youth sports.
According to city documents, BCLL started missing their utility payments in 2021 and racked up more than $13,000 in special assessment taxes before earning their tax-exempt status. Although the property’s water lines have been shut off, the city still charges the organization for storm drain runoff. A single street lamp provides the only light source at the property and racks up an Xcel Energy bill.
Brenny said community members looking to help the organization, financially or otherwise, should reach out to the Brooklyn Center Little League Facebook page or send an email to bcllmnbaseball@gmail.com .
“Lots and lots of past members and parents, they all want the same thing. They want the ball fields to remain open,” she said. "Let's work together. Let's get this board up and running. Let's get committed to the kids and to baseball again.”
